approachQuestion.prompt:
Keep arrival order among equal scores

A contest returns entrant IDs ordered by score descending. Entrants with equal scores must stay in their original input order. Return all IDs; do not modify the input. IDs are unique.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; integer scores; comparisons constant time.

Examples: [(A,8),(B,5),(C,8)] → [A,C,B]. [(X,4),(Y,4)] → [X,Y].

Choose a valid method that meets the full contract with the least unnecessary work.
constraints: The stated input/output and mutation requirements apply to every option.

options.text: Use a stable descending sort by score on a copy, then emit IDs.
options.feedback: Stability preserves original relative order for every tied score.

options.text: Sort by score descending and ID ascending.
options.feedback: A tie must follow arrival order, which need not match ID order.
This places lower scores first, reversing the required primary order.

options.text: Sort by score descending, then restore input order among every equal-score group with a separate scan of all original records.
options.feedback: This can produce the required order, but repeated searches for tied records are unnecessary when the sort itself is stable.

feedback.reason: Equal scores must keep arrival order, so the sorting method's stability is part of correctness.
details: Copy the records, apply a stable comparison sort by descending score, and emit IDs in sorted order.
Equal scores must keep arrival order, so the sorting method's stability is part of correctness. A descending comparator alone does not guarantee that order under an unstable sort.
“Use a stable descending sort by score on a copy, then emit IDs.”: Stability preserves original relative order for every tied score.
“Sort by score descending and ID ascending.”: A tie must follow arrival order, which need not match ID order.
“Sort only by score ascending.”: This places lower scores first, reversing the required primary order.

“Sort by score descending, then restore input order among every equal-score group with a separate scan of all original records.”: This can produce the required order, but repeated searches for tied records are unnecessary when the sort itself is stable.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed revealed method, choose its tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds. Count copies, sorting buffer and recursion stack; exclude caller input and returned output. Comparison merge sort uses a linear buffer; comparisons and moves are constant-time.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space

feedback.reason: Stable comparison sorting orders copied records without discarding arrival ties.
details: Comparison merge sort takes O(n log n) worst-case time; its copied records and merge buffer require O(n) auxiliary space. The recursion stack is O(log n), within O(n). Linear time omits sorting, quadratic time overstates the sort cost; constant space omits the buffer.
